issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is a highly specific trigger that is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type of police violence as described here. The other trigger, threat, memory, and strategy items all center on generalized danger/hypervigilance and perpetrator-related reminders, not exposure/undress themes. Without any corroborating memory or appraisal content about forced stripping, searches, or sexualized humiliation, this item looks clinically mismatched.

Nothing in the triggers, threat, or memory items suggests the traumatic event involved a church, faith community, or religion-linked cue. In this profile it appears disconnected from the identified trauma network and is hard to explain clinically as part of the same PTSD presentation.

vignette:
The night it happened, Nina was off duty, walking home from a late shift. A patrol car pulled up, and two officers got out. She didn't register the mistake until the first one shoved her against the wall, his hand flat on her sternum, pinning her there while the other yelled questions she couldn't follow. She was wearing her paramedic jacket; they said she matched a description. The whole thing lasted maybe four minutes, but the sequence has never made sense to her since. She cannot put the memories in the right order - the flash of the badge, the gravel scraping her cheek, the sound of her own voice saying "I'm a medic" over and over - it all arrives at once, jumbled and unfinished. When she tries to explain what happened, she loses the thread mid-sentence and cannot finish, the words dissolving into a vague gesture.

In the weeks that followed, Nina found that the memory did not stay in the past. It felt like it was happening right now, the pressure of the officer's hand still present on her chest, the shouting still ringing in her ears. This made her hypervigilant. She began to scan her surroundings constantly for signs of danger, always choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected she felt - back to the wall, exit in sight. The memory itself triggered a visceral physical response: she would feel suddenly nauseous, a wave of sickness rising without warning, especially when stress accumulated. And any unexpected touch - a colleague tapping her shoulder, a patient grabbing her arm - made her react with alarm, a full-body flinch she could not control.

The hypervigilance, in turn, intensified the memory. The more she scanned, the more the event replayed itself, fragmented and vivid. She started to suppress her anger entirely, never allowing herself to feel or express it, because she was certain that if she let even a fraction of that rage surface, she would lose control completely. This suppression came at a cost: the unexpressed anger looped back and made the memory feel more present, more urgent, as if the event were still unresolved and still threatening. It also fed her scanning. She became more vigilant, more on edge, because she was holding so much inside.

Nina's avoidance grew systematic. She began to avoid anything that reminded her of the person who harmed her - a specific cologne, the model of patrol car, the sound of a radio crackling. More broadly, she avoided being around people in authority or uniform, which became a serious problem at work. As a paramedic, she regularly interacted with police officers at scenes. She started requesting different assignments, switching shifts to avoid certain co-responder teams. Her colleagues noticed she was quieter, jumpier, and she withdrew from the station's social life entirely.

Six months on, Nina's life has narrowed. She no longer sits in the break room; she eats in her car. She has been late to calls because she took a longer route to avoid a police substation. Her divorce, already strained before the incident, was finalized last month - her ex-husband said she was "impossible to live with," always flinching, always watching the door. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week: a patient's family member touched her elbow to thank her, and she screamed. The attending officer looked at her strangely. She realized she could not keep working this way. She is terrified that the memory will never settle, that she will always be this reactive, but she is also afraid of what will happen if she stops suppressing - afraid the anger will be bottomless.
